newsitem.title: BELGIUM: New BBL chief sees "stand-alone" future for bank.
newsitem.headline: New BBL chief sees "stand-alone" future for bank.

text.p: The new chief executive officer of Banque Bruxelles Lambert, a bank which has long been the focus of merger talk, crushed speculation on Wednesday, saying he saw his bank's future in a "stand alone" perspective.
"Our policy is a 'stand-alone' one. BBL is a happy, though attentive, bachelor," Michel Tilmant, chief executive since January 1, told a news conference about 1996 earnings.
It was Tilmant's first public statement on alliance policy, which had been long awaited by financial markets.
His predecessor, Daniel Cardon, had repeatedly said that he wanted a partner for the bank to face the challenges of the European single currency.

"Our bank is capable of building its future alone. But if any opportunities arise, we will definitely look at them," he said. He added any alliance would have to respect the rights of customers, personnel, shareholders and the broader society.

Asked about a proposal last year by holding company Ste Generale de Belgique (SGB) to merge SGB unit Generale Bank with BBL, Tilmant said: "I was in favour of this project. But for reasons we all know this could not proceed."
SGB chief executive Etienne Davignon said last year that a Generale Bank-BBL merger had been blocked by BBL minority shareholder Internationale Nederlanden Groep (ING).

Asked whether a merger with Generale Bank would not by definition cost jobs and lead to branch closures Tilmant said: "A merger could have advantages for the domestic network, we would increase our marketing power."
Tilmant insisted that he was not at odds with his predecessor about BBL's future.
"The sole difference is that last year, there was a concrete project. This is now in the fridge," he said.

Paribas Bank Belgium chief executive officer Philippe Romagnoli said last month that at least three top Belgian banks should merge to create a player that is fit to tackle the larger market created by the single currency. Cardon had also repeatedly said he thought BBL was too small.
"There is no critical mass or optimal size. If you want to be a big universal bank, size is important. If you want to be a small asset manager, then it is not," he said.
BBL shares have carried a takeover premium for several years, as the market considers that the bank's disparate shareholdership structure makes it ripe for a merger operation.
At the end of 1996, holding company Groupe Bruxelles Lambert (GBL), traditionaly the leading shareholder in BBL, had a stake of 12.44 percent.
GBL last year signed a three-way shareholder pact for the control of BBL with insurer Royale Belge, which holds 12.37 percent, and Credit Communal, which owns 12.33 percent.
Dutch ING owns a 13.40 percent stake and controls the voting rights over another 6.73 percent.
BBL said in a statement group net profit rose 15.1 percent to 10.29 billion francs, from 8.94 billion.
Tilmant added that 1997 profit growth would be more modest.
BBL shares ended 3.4 percent lower at 8,190 francs.
